verdict: OK to lend in Mundra power — back the PPA-backed generation and its fuel/OM supply chain, not merchant or discom-receivable-heavy exposure.
title: Mundra Power Generation & Distribution: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**A power plant is a fuel-to-cash converter: coal in, units out, billed to a buyer under a PPA.** Cash sits in two places — the fuel/working-capital cycle on the way in, and the receivable from the offtaker on the way out. Mundra is India's imported-coal hub, so the plant's cost base is dollar-linked coal while its tariff is rupee and regulated; that mismatch is the whole credit story. **The single biggest risk is not generation, it is who pays and when.** Rating work on thermal producers is explicit that liquidity is judged on cash collections from the counterparty, DSRA availability and working-capital limit use [8]; a peer case shows collection periods stretching past 400 days on weak discoms [10]. So when a proposal lands, check the offtaker's payment record first; if the buyer is a weak state discom, ask for the last 24 months of actual receipt dates, not billed dates. ## What has changed now
**The local news is a restart story, and it is positive but early.** Tata Power is nearing restart of its imported coal-based Mundra plant after Gujarat PPA approval, with a revised agreement enabling coal cost pass-through [3]. That pass-through is the credit fix — it moves fuel-price risk off the borrower's P&L. **Treat [3] as a single trade-press report, not confirmation of commissioning.** Peer results are strong: Vedanta Power posted record quarterly sales with EBITDA up 45% sequentially and margins at 14.5% [5], and separately reported 122% EBITDA growth to INR 421 crore on revenue of INR 2,908 crore [6]; Adani Power runs 18.33 GW with 95% of capacity tied to long-term PPAs [7]. Coal India's Q2 FY27 net profit rose 57% YoY to Rs 6,547 crore even as target prices were cut [4] — fuel is available and priced, not scarce. **Demand is real: Gujarat electricity demand is up 11.0% Apr-to-date versus India's 9.5% [D].**

## Where to grow
**Pursue the annuity around the plant, not the plant's merchant upside.** Target: (a) coal handling, ash utilisation and O&M contractors with assigned PPA-backed receivables; (b) transmission and distribution EPC and material suppliers to Gujarat discoms, where GST collections are running +11.9% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1% [D]; (c) captive and group-captive generators selling into Gujarat's 11.0% demand growth [D]. **Avoid pure merchant generators with no PPA and borrowers whose sole offtaker is a stretched discom** — the 400-day collection precedent [10] is the cautionary case. Note the macro gap: bank credit is +22.9% YoY against activity of +9.5% [D], so pricing is competitive; do not chase volume into weak structures. ## How to grow safely
**Structure against the receivable, not the asset.** Take assignment of PPA cash flows or an escrow of offtaker payments; require DSRA and minimum coverage covenants in line with rating practice [8]. **Every month take: generation and PLF, billed versus collected units, receivable ageing by offtaker, coal inventory days, working-capital limit utilisation, and DSRA balance.** If collection days rise two months running, cut limits and move to cash-collateralised lending. ## Early-warning signs
- **Receivable days stretching** (monthly): two consecutive rises -> freeze new limits, re-price. - **Coal cost pass-through delayed or disputed** (quarterly): any PPA renegotiation news -> stop disbursement until order copy seen. - **PLF falling below plan** (monthly): two quarters of shortfall -> reassess debt-service cover. - **Restart slippage at Mundra** (quarterly): commissioning date pushed again -> treat [3] as unconfirmed and hold.

two quarters of shortfall -> reassess debt-service cover
